article_title: I CAN Learn® Primary Mathematics
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2017, July). Primary Mathematics intervention report: I CAN Learn®. Retrieved from https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Five-part self-paced mastery lesson structure
description: I CAN Learn® lessons follow a repeating five-part design in which instruction is delivered by software and advancement is gated by demonstrated mastery. The curriculum studied included "109 lessons, each of which has a five-part format that includes a warm-up activity, lesson presentation, journal activity, guided practice, and a quiz to ensure mastery of the lesson content". Students complete lessons individually at their own pace using interactive software with a virtual teacher that presents multimodal lessons and demonstrates problem solving when students make errors, while the classroom teacher supports students with the lessons.
requirements: Computer equipment, desks, and electrical connectivity in classrooms; the developer provided maintenance and technical and instructional support to teachers
constraints: The study did not specify which edition of the curriculum was used
examples: In the reviewed quasi-experiment, intervention students used this lesson format as the primary source of math instruction for the entire academic school year in 12 to 14 middle schools
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2017, July). Primary Mathematics intervention report: I CAN Learn®. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/676

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Tithi, S.D., Alam, N., Yasir, T., Shi, Y., Tian, X., Chi, M., Barnes, T. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07308
title: ICAP-based operationalization of cognitive engagement levels through worked example types in an ITS
description: This framework maps the ICAP engagement modes onto concrete problem representations in an intelligent logic tutor. Problem Solving is treated as "Interactive in the ICAP framework, since students receive explicit accuracy feedback on each step"; Guided worked examples, adapted from the Parsons format with subgoal structure, represent the "activeengagement level in ICAP"; and Buggy worked examples, containing expert-designed errors students must find and fix, represent the "constructiveengagement level in ICAP". The article uses this mapping as the theoretically grounded basis for adaptive scaffolding policies that select among engagement levels.
requirements: The tutor must provide problem-solving interleaved with the two worked-example types, and the ICAP level of each activity must be assigned; the article notes that "defining the ICAP level of a learning activity is non-trivial" because feedback-driven reflection could make either type more interactive.
constraints: The operationalization was implemented and evaluated in one logic tutor in an undergraduate discrete math course; the authors state the design "should be replicated in other problem-solving domains" to establish generalizability.
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete math / computer science course
target_learning_goals: propositional logic proof construction and rule application
examples: In the study tutor, Guided examples presented partial solutions with missing node connections students complete by applying rules, while Buggy examples presented solutions with expert-designed bugs students identify and correct.
key_sources: Tithi, S.D., Alam, N., Yasir, T., Shi, Y., Tian, X., Chi, M., Barnes, T. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07308

article_title: Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy
citation: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256
title: ICAP framework: Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive hierarchy of learning modes
description: The ICAP framework distinguishes observable states of learning engagement, allowing more effective assessment of educational activities and stable cross-study comparison of collaborative learning. In its hierarchy, "interactive activities that engage learners in instructional settings to co-construct new knowledge yield the best learning outcomes." The interactive mode involves developing knowledge beyond provided materials by asking questions, giving and receiving feedback, and incorporating others' ideas; it is followed by the constructive mode, then active (applying knowledge to similar but non-identical scenarios), then passive activities like listening or reading, which are less effective. The review uses ICAP to classify each included study's CL activity, partners, and modes.
requirements: Activities must be classifiable into the four observable learning modes using the modes' classifying verbs
constraints: Passive activities are less effective because they require similar cues or contexts for recall, per the framework the review cites
target_learners: learners of all ages in AI literacy settings, from children to professionals
examples: The review classified each of the nine studies' activities, e.g. a card game where players combine cards creatively (constructive: strategize play; interactive: respond to challenged plays)
key_sources: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256

article_title: Would You Let a Humanoid Play Storytelling With Your Child? A Usability Study on LLM-Powered Narrative Human-Robot Interaction
citation: Maria Lombardi, Carmela Calabrese, Davide Ghiglino, Caterina Foglino, Davide De Tommaso, Giulia Da Lisca, Lorenzo Natale, Agnieszka Wykowska. (2025). Would you let a humanoid play storytelling with your child? A usability study on LLM-powered narrative Human-Robot Interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02505
title: iCub LLM-powered narrative HRI system architecture
description: A companion-like social robotic platform in which the iCub humanoid and a human partner co-create a story in turn from pictures on nine soft cubes, each story built on a sequence of three cubes. Perception modules run online from the robot's own eye camera: face recognition (OpenPose, FaceNet embeddings, an SVM classifier), mutual-gaze detection from 19 facial key-points, online-trainable object detection, and zero-shot sticker description via ChatGPT-4o as VLM. Story generation uses ChatGPT-4o as LLM with ad-hoc prompts, plus speech transcription and synthesis, all orchestrated by a finite state machine over the YARP middleware. The article states the design 'allows to change stimuli fast without training the system again, representing a future easily adaptive tool for therapists.'
requirements: A local network connecting the robot to a GPU-equipped workstation and client laptop running the perception and generation modules
Online-trainable perception so the system is not constrained to a pre-trained subset of partners or objects
constraints: All perception uses only RGB frames from iCub's eye, without external sensors
Latency from external services such as ChatGPT and slow motor movement affected perceived efficiency
target_learners: children under 10, including children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (intended end users)
target_learning_goals: communication skills, turn taking, autonomy, and narrative expression through collaborative storytelling
examples: In the validation experiment each adult participant invented three stories with iCub, exchanging cubes in turn while the robot detected stickers, generated story pieces and gave positive feedback.

article_title: Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective
citation: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453
title: ICE-T: a didactic framework integrating intermodal transfer, computational thinking, and explanatory thinking for ML education
description: ICE-T is a multi-faceted didactic framework for teaching machine learning whose name mnemonically captures its components: Intermodal Transfer grounded in Bruner's enactive-iconic-symbolic principle, Computational Thinking operationalized through the Use-Modify-Create progression, and Explanatory Thinking supported by the PETSP-ML process model. The article states the framework "unifies the three didactic facets described above into a coherent, actionable framework for ML education". The three facets are treated as orthogonal dimensions of a single learning unit: EIS modes structure how a concept is represented, UMC structures the degree of student autonomy, and PETSP-ML structures the temporal sequence, with which combinations are realized left as a deliberate educator design decision.
requirements: Educators deliberately decide which combinations of representational mode, UMC stage, and process phase are realized at each point of a learning unit
constraints: The connection between ICE-T and trust calibration is, at this stage, theoretical and has not itself been evaluated; its empirical grounding is limited to the K-12 landscape
target_learners: K-12 students with little or no prior exposure to programming
examples: A decision-tree animal classification unit: students physically sort animal cards (enactive), construct a visual decision tree on a whiteboard (iconic), implement classification rules in code (symbolic), progress through Use, Modify, and Create within each modality, and follow the PETSP-ML stages from task understanding to model training and evaluation
key_sources: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453

article_title: Patterns of Learner-AI Interaction and Academic Performance in an Object-Oriented Programming Course
citation: Marina Lepp. (2026). Patterns of Learner–AI Interaction and Academic Performance in an Object-Oriented Programming Course. IEEE Frontiers in Education (FIE) 2026 Conference.
title: ICAP framework as a lens for interpreting learner–AI interaction patterns
description: The article uses the ICAP framework, which "distinguishes between passive, active, constructive, and interactive engagement", to interpret why different GenAI usage patterns relate differently to learning. Zero and Low usage patterns are read as predominantly active engagement without AI mediation, the "Smart" high usage pattern as closer to "constructive engagement that supports sense -making", and Very high usage as frequent interaction that remains largely active rather than constructive. The framework is applied as an interpretive lens rather than tested empirically.
requirements: Analyses must capture what learners do with AI (e.g., explanation seeking versus solution generation), not just usage frequency
constraints: The article notes ICAP has only recently begun to inform research on GenAI use in programming education
target_learners: undergraduate novice programmers in OOP courses
examples: The discussion maps the five identified usage clusters onto ICAP engagement modes, treating explanation-focused use as constructive and very high-volume use as largely active

article_title: Towards Self-Referential Analytic Assessment: A Profile-Based Approach to L2 Writing Evaluation with LLMs
citation: Stefano Bannò, Kate Knill, Mark Gales. (2026). Towards Self-Referential Analytic Assessment: A Profile-Based Approach to L2 Writing Evaluation with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04298
title: ICNALE Global Rating Archive (GRA) dataset
description: A publicly available L2 learner dataset derived from a subset of ICNALE, containing learner essays and speeches annotated from an English as a Lingua Franca assessment perspective that evaluates English as a communicative tool among non-native speakers rather than against native-speaker norms. Although relatively small (N=140 essays used here), "each essay has been annotated by 80 trained raters", yielding a fully crossed rater-essay design comprising 123,195 ratings. Essays carry holistic scores (0-100) and ten analytic aspects (0-10) grouped under Language, Content, and Attitude macro-aspects.
requirements: Rasch-based rater selection and score calibration to mitigate substantial rater disagreement
constraints: Data focus on Asian learners within an ELF framework, so generalisation to other L1 backgrounds or L2s requires further research
target_learning_goals: Holistic and analytic assessment of L2 English writing proficiency
examples: The study uses only the essay section, with four anomalous scores recoded and five missing ratings noted

article_title: With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education
citation: Rummel, N., Nachtigall, V., & Panadero, E. (2026). “With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook”: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education.
title: ICAP framework: four modes of cognitive engagement from passive to interactive
description: The ICAP framework, as deployed in this article, distinguishes four modes of cognitive engagement — Passive, Active, Constructive, and Interactive — that differ in the cognitive effort learners invest in modifying existing and creating new learning products. The authors map each of their four Thermomix/generative-AI use cases onto one mode, from passively following guided instructions to co-constructing knowledge in dialogue. They use it to argue that "higher modes of engagement leading to superior learning outcomes" anchors the analogy between cooking and learning with AI.
requirements: Distinguishing use cases by the degree of cognitive effort learners invest, from receiving outputs to collaboratively co-constructing knowledge
constraints: The article treats the mode-outcome ordering as a hypothesized assumption of the framework, not as a result tested in this paper
target_learners: students using generative AI tools in educational settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful cognitive engagement with learning tasks
examples: The article assigns its four scenarios to Passive/Substitution, Active/Augmentation, Constructive/Modification, and Interactive/Redefinition in Table 1

article_title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
citation: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823
title: The ICAP Framework: A Taxonomy of Four Modes of Cognitive Engagement Based on Overt Behaviors
description: The ICAP framework is a taxonomy that differentiates students' cognitive engagement into four modes based on the overt behaviors they display while learning: Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive. The framework proposes that "engagement behaviors can be categorized and differentiated into one of four modes" and that each mode corresponds to different underlying knowledge-change processes. It provides "specific domain-general guidelines for creating more engaging lessons as well as modifying existing activities to increase engagement, using simple overt measures of behavior to assess the level to which students are engaged." The framework is intended to help teachers and educational designers classify and design learning activities.
requirements: Overt behaviors must be content relevant to be classified into a mode
A content analysis of learners' responses is necessary to confirm the actual mode of an activity
constraints: Overt behaviors are a proxy, not a perfect measure — students may be covertly processing deeply while appearing passive
Boundaries between modes are not totally rigid; some activities fall on the boundary between two categories
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes across subject matters through differentiated cognitive engagement
examples: While reading a text, students can be reading silently (passive), underlining (active), taking notes in one's own words (constructive), or asking a friend questions about the materials (interactive)
key_sources: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823

article_title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
citation: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823
title: Knowledge-Change Processes Underlying Each ICAP Mode: Storing, Integrating, Inferring, and Co-Inferring
description: The article postulates four broad types of knowledge-change processes, each associated with one mode of engagement. Passive engagement involves isolated "storing" of information in an encapsulated manner without integration with prior knowledge. Active engagement involves "integrating" processes in which manipulated information activates relevant prior knowledge and new information is assimilated into the activated schema. Constructive engagement involves "inferring" processes including inducing, deducing, revising, repairing, reorganizing, and reflecting. Interactive engagement involves "co-inferring" processes where "each learner infers new knowledge from activated and integrated knowledge and iteratively infers knowledge with new inputs from conversational partner(s)."
requirements: Knowledge-change processes are assumed to be relatively distinct from task-specific learning processes
The same set of knowledge-change processes is assumed for all activities within a given mode
constraints: The authors state their main assumption is not whether they have postulated the processes accurately but rather that they are relatively different for each mode
target_learning_goals: understanding how different engagement modes produce different changes in knowledge structures
examples: A student who read about blood clots could recite the textbook explanation but gave a contradictory answer when asked to use her own theory, suggesting the new ideas were stored in an isolated or encapsulated way
key_sources: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823

article_title: An observation study of reading instruction provided to elementary students with learning disabilities in the resource room
citation: Swanson, E. A., & Vaughn, S. (2010). An Observation Study of Reading Instruction Provided to Elementary Students With Learning Disabilities in the Resource Room. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20484
title: Instructional Content Emphasis Instrument–Revised (ICE-R) for observing reading instruction
description: The ICE-R is a multidimensional, taxonomically designed observation instrument for coding teachers' reading instruction. It yields "multidimensional descriptions of reading instruction," time allocated to instructional components, student grouping patterns, level of student engagement, and instructional quality. Dimension A codes the main instructional category (e.g., word study, comprehension, fluency), Dimension B the subcategory, and Dimension C grouping practices. Engagement is coded on a 3-point Likert scale and quality on a 4-point scale based on indicators such as explicit instruction and teacher modeling. In this study observers received 6 hours of training and reached 100% agreement on all ICE-R sections before data collection.
requirements: Trained observers; the study required coders to reach at least 90% agreement on a training video and 100% agreement on all ICE-R sections prior to data collection.
constraints: Quality and engagement ratings depend on observer coding of instructional events, with the article noting observer effects such as conspicuous observation as a threat.
target_learners: Elementary students with learning disabilities in resource-room settings
target_learning_goals: Describing and evaluating the quality of reading instruction across phonological awareness, word study, fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary
examples: Observers coded 2,178 minutes of reading instruction across 10 resource-room teachers over three consecutive observation days per classroom.
key_sources: Swanson, E. A., & Vaughn, S. (2010). An Observation Study of Reading Instruction Provided to Elementary Students With Learning Disabilities in the Resource Room. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20484

article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: The ICAP framework as a conceptual pillar for collaborative learning benefits in CSCL
description: The article presents ICAP (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Chi et al., 2018) as providing "conceptual and evidential support for the benefits of collaborative learning over and above all other modes of learning". Within its taxonomy, interactive (collaborative) question generation is expected to lead to the highest learning gains, above constructive individual generation and better than active and passive modes. The article argues that, while not specific to computer-supported collaboration, ICAP might well serve as a conceptual pillar for the CSCL field.
requirements: The framework lens implies designing activities that push learners from passive and active modes toward constructive and interactive modes of engagement.
constraints: The article notes ICAP has so far hardly been used in CSCL research, and that closer attention to the role of technology in learning and collaboration would advance it.
target_learners: visitors and learners in CSCL contexts, including museum group visitors
target_learning_goals: maximizing learning gains through interactive modes of cognitive engagement
examples: The museum study used the ICAP taxonomy as its theoretical framework to justify comparing interactive versus constructive question-generation modes.
key_sources: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6

article_title: Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
citation: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi. (2025). Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09456-5
title: ICAP framework as a theory of four hierarchical engagement modes applied to CSCL
description: The article uses the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) as its theoretical model for evaluating cognitive engagement during collaboration. It "classifies learning activities into four modes—passive, active, constructive, and interactive—on the basis of the learner’s level of engagement." In the interactive mode learners coconstruct knowledge through dialogue and coinference; constructive mode involves generating inferences that elaborate understanding. The study operationalizes ICAP through a coding schema of utterance indicators (Table 1) combined with epistemic network analysis to capture engagement temporally.
requirements: Observable discourse data coded against an ICAP-based rubric; at least three codes are needed to build an ENA model
constraints: ICAP coding reliability in this study was Krippendorff's α = 0.68, described as consistent only to some extent
target_learners: older adult learners in lifelong learning settings
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding through collaborative elaboration of knowledge
examples: The study coded utterances from paired concept-map explanation tasks into active, constructive, and interactive indicators and ran ENA on the resulting networks

article_title: The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study
citation: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09374-1
title: ICAP-CG: an ICAP-based coding guide for assessing indirect SRL promotion from lesson tasks
description: The ICAP-CG is an observation protocol developed in prior work (Vosniadou et al., 2023) that codes lesson tasks minute-by-minute into Passive, Active, Active/Collaborative, Constructive, and Interactive engagement modes based on the verbs teachers use in task instructions. "The ICAP-CG was used to examine the transcripts of the filmed lessons on a minute-by-minute basis and to identify the lesson tasks." An Active/Collaborative code was added for cases where teachers asked students to work together using Active rather than Constructive or Interactive verbs.
requirements: Requires filmed lesson transcripts with timestamps; coders identify lesson tasks and assign engagement codes from teacher instruction verbs and student activity
constraints: Students were assumed to engage in the tasks as described by the teachers' instructions, with student codes adjusted only when the transcript showed a discrepancy
target_learning_goals: assessing opportunities for indirect promotion of self-regulated learning
examples: Applied to 107 lesson tasks across 898 minutes of observation in 23 classrooms, reaching 93% agreement and Cohen's Kappa of 0.86 between coders
key_sources: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). article_title: From Passive to Metacognitive: The Role of Mode of Engagement in Enabling Lasting Learning Using Digital Media
citation: Yoana Omarchevska, Brendan A. Schuetze, Juliane Richter, Sascha Schanze, Nina Ulrich, Katharina Scheiter. (2026). From Passive to Metacognitive: The Role of Mode of Engagement in Enabling Lasting Learning Using Digital Media. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10120-z
title: Extension of the ICAP framework adding metacognitive engagement as an additional mode
description: The article proposes extending the ICAP framework (passive, active, constructive, interactive modes of cognitive engagement) with metacognitive engagement, operationalized as the frequency of making judgments of learning. The authors "propose metacognitive engagement as an additional mode of engagement", arguing it is particularly relevant for self-regulated, individual learning with open-ended digital environments. Their findings that profiles differing mainly in metacognitive engagement showed the largest knowledge differences support this extension correlationally.
requirements: A learning environment that logs or affords observable metacognitive activities such as judgments of learning
constraints: The empirical support is correlational, from a single classroom study with one digital textbook
target_learners: secondary school students (eighth grade) learning science individually with digital media
target_learning_goals: durable domain-specific chemistry knowledge (particle model of matter)
examples: In the eChemBook, students could optionally rate on a traffic light scale how well they could explain each unit and check which concepts they could explain

citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: ICAP framework as a lens for examining instructional support and manipulatives efficacy
description: The commentary proposes Chi's Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework as a potential framework for examining instructional support and manipulatives efficacy. As printed, "The ICAP model differentiates learning tasks by categorizing learning activities as interactive, constructive, active, or passive and links these behaviors to different cognitive processes". Systematically examining learning tasks within this framework may identify specific recommendations for producing high performance on learning outcomes.
requirements: Learning tasks must be categorizable as interactive, constructive, active, or passive
target_learners: Classroom learners across manipulative-based instruction contexts
target_learning_goals: Performance on multiple learning outcome types
examples: The commentary suggests future research focus on quantitative and qualitative factors of instructional activities, including modality of outcome tasks, examined within the ICAP framework

article_title: Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Juliette C. Désiron, Julien Venni, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2026). Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10138-3
title: Integrated Cognitive-Affective Model of Learning with Media (ICALM)
description: ICALM (Plass & Kaplan, 2016) refines the cognitive-affective theory of multimedia learning by attributing the induction of positive affective states to multimedia characteristics. The review describes how "Multimedia stimuli engage both cognitive and affective resources, with these processes being closely linked and interacting reciprocally—emotions influence content processing and vice versa". Integration into a coherent mental model in long-term memory includes affect in the form of emotion schemas. The review uses ICALM, with CTML and CATML, as its theoretical grounding for how visual features guide attention, load, affect and motivation.
requirements: Theoretical grounding assumes design elements can induce affective states that interact reciprocally with cognitive processing during selection, organization, and integration.
target_learners: multimedia learners in the reviewed studies (school and higher education)
target_learning_goals: retention, transfer and comprehension of instructional multimedia content

article_title: Probing boundary conditions of Productive Failure and analyzing the role of young students’ collaboration
citation: Claudia Mazziotti, Nikol Rummel, Anne Deiglmayr and Katharina Loibl. (2019). Probing boundary conditions of Productive Failure and analyzing the role of young students' collaboration. npj Science of Learning 4:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0041-5
title: ICAP framework as a coding lens for collaborative engagement in Productive Failure
description: The article uses the Interactive–Constructive–Active–Passive (ICAP) framework by Chi and colleagues as a tool for aligning students' overt learning activities with underlying cognitive processes during collaborative problem solving. It "can serve as a tool for aligning different kinds of students' overt learning activities" — from passively listening to interactively co-constructing solution ideas — "to underlying cognitive processes". The framework proposes a hierarchy (I > C > A > P) in which higher engagement levels are more conducive to learning. The authors coded 5074 utterances from PF-Coll dyads using six categories derived from ICAP and broader collaborative-learning literature.
requirements: Coding requires transcripts of recorded dialogs and a coding scheme differentiating interactive, constructive, active, coordinative, back channeling, and off-task utterances
constraints: The authors found no clear superiority of interactive processes in their study, and note the ICAP categories may be too broad to capture nuances of collaborative learning
target_learners: elementary school students working in dyads
examples: Coders classified students' verbal utterances from audiotaped dyad dialogs, using a conservative approach choosing the lower code in cases of ambiguity (ICC absolute = 0.92)
key_sources: Claudia Mazziotti, Nikol Rummel, Anne Deiglmayr and Katharina Loibl. (2019). Probing boundary conditions of Productive Failure and analyzing the role of young students' collaboration. npj Science of Learning 4:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0041-5

article_title: Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON
citation: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9
title: ICON system: dynamic intracultural contextualisation architecture for ILEs
description: ICON (Instructional Cultural cONtextualisation) models conceptual and linguistic variations across the subcultures in a student's background and generates culturally adapted educational content dynamically. Its architecture comprises four components: "a Contextual Student Model, Contextual Element Repository, Cultural Linguistics Adapter, and a Controller". The CSM estimates metacultural competence via weighted rule-based membership scores; the repository selects culturally appropriate images and terms using the CERA ontology; the adapter varies formality (acrolect/mesolect/basilect) and substitutes localized vocabulary measured as sentence distortion; the Controller links ICON to the host ILE.
requirements: Requires detailed student demographic data plus national-level census and statistical data organised into an ontological structure to estimate cultural group membership strengths.
Requires ontological structures and Semantic Web techniques for meaningful semantic contextualisation, as the authors concur with prior work.
constraints: The Cultural Linguistics Adapter's formality variation is limited to English-based Creoles and to grammatical transformation rules.
In the reported work the modelling range was fully developed for only Trinidadian culture.
target_learners: students from diverse subcultures within a society, exemplified by Trinidadian university students
target_learning_goals: adapting educational content (problem descriptions, images, feedback, hints) to students' cultural backgrounds while preserving the learning context
examples: For a sample student with a strong Roman Catholic background and mixed ancestry, ICON recommended references like 'bake and shark', 'doubles' and 'Angostura bitters', and transformed 'John gave away free biscuits' into 'John gave away free Angostura bitters'.
key_sources: Phaedra Mohammed & Permanand Mohan. (2015). Dynamic Cultural Contextualisation of Educational Content in Intelligent Learning Environments using ICON. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:249–270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0033-9

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: ICAP-based operationalisation of learner engagement categories in AVW-Space
description: The article operationalises the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) for video-based learning, classifying overt learner behaviours into Passive, Active, Constructive and Interactive modes, with learning effectiveness increasing from passive to interactive. Because AVW-Space did not support collaboration, the Interactive mode was excluded, yielding categories of Passive learners (watch but write no comments), Active learners (watch and write comments), and Constructive learners (comments add something new). The article quotes the underlying evidence: "as students become more engaged, starting from the passive mode to the interactive mode, the learning effectiveness increases; i.e. Passive < Active < Constructive < Interactive". In the reported studies Active and Constructive learners were not distinguished because the system could not analyse comment text.
requirements: Interaction logs and comments that allow overt behaviours to be classified into ICAP categories
constraints: AVW-Space did not support collaboration, so the Interactive mode was not considered; AL and CL were not distinguished in the reported studies
target_learners: university students watching videos in self-study settings
target_learning_goals: increasing cognitive engagement during video-based learning of presentation skills
examples: Passive learners log on and watch videos but write no comments; Active learners write comments on points in the videos; Constructive learners' comments or aspect use add something new, such as reflecting on past experience

article_title: High-quality digital distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures: Does familiarity with technology matter?
citation: Fütterer, T., Hoch, E., Lachner, A., Scheiter, K., & Stürmer, K. (2023). High-quality digital distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures: Does familiarity with technology matter? Computers & Education, 199, 104788. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104788
title: ICAP hypothesis applied to digital distance teaching
description: The study applies the Interactive Constructive Active Passive (ICAP) hypothesis (Chi & Wylie, 2014) to operationalize student-observed learning activities in digital distance teaching. The framework predicts that "as students become more engaged with the learning materials, from passive to active to constructive to interactive, their learning will increase." The study used a slider with four anchor points corresponding to ICAP levels to capture student-observed learning activities across 14 technology types, weighted by frequency of use.
requirements: Observable learning activities must be linked to underlying cognitive learning processes, as the framework assumes "mental processes […] can be inferred from behavioral indices"
constraints: The framework was applied via student self-reports rather than observational coding
target_learning_goals: Effort in learning during digital distance teaching

It organizes the literature around how ICT is deployed with gifted learners, the outcomes reported, and the methods used, providing a structured map of a scattered field. The review frames ICT as a resource that can enrich learning for high-ability students while noting uneven evidence quality.

title: Three-level iceberg organization of TB health educator competency: visible competencies, supporting competencies, and core drivers
description: The article organizes its seven-dimension competency system using the Iceberg Competency Model into three levels. Above the waterline are "Visible Competencies": professional knowledge base, communication and health education skills, and clinical practice and problem-solving skills, described as directly observable and measurable. Supporting competencies (learning and development, collaboration and resource integration) bridge to the deepest level, "Core Drivers": professionalism and self-management, and research and innovation competence, which the authors describe as hardest to cultivate but most enduring. The dimensions are presented as progressive and mutually reinforcing.

constraints: The three-level organization is the authors' interpretive mapping onto the Iceberg Competency Model, not an empirically tested structure

target_learning_goals: Professional competency development for TB health education practice

description: The review uses the ICAP framework by Chi and Wylie, which "distinguishes four modes of engagement: interactive, constructive, active and passive," to classify wound care teaching methods. It suggests "students' learning experience improves if students are actively engaging with the presented content," with interactive and constructive modes hypothesised as most effective. Most reviewed interventions used interactive or constructive modes such as hands-on clinical application and case-based discussions.

constraints: The review notes it remains uncertain whether actively engaging approaches lead to better results than lectures, as the ICAP framework suggests

description: iCubed@UMBC is a five-year NSF-funded investigation (Project Number 1038170, awarded 2010) into cost-effective, scalable strategies to increase STEM degree completion at UMBC. Eligible consenting freshmen are "randomly assigned into five separate groups": high-status faculty mentoring, professional staff mentoring, active-learning discussion sections in CASTLE, study-group assistance, and a control group offered a $50 bookstore gift card. Participation spans fall and spring semesters across three cohorts (2011-2012, 2012-2013, 2013-2014 academic years).

description: The article's theory of change posits that enacting the five standards of effective teaching generates a sufficiently high level of responsive assistance for ELLs that increases student learning. description: The article recommends that ICT use in classrooms for students with hearing impairment be paired with pedagogy that actively involves learners, since technology alone does not guarantee learning. The recommendation follows directly from the study's finding that ICT-based instruction improved economics learning outcomes.

citation: Portes, P. R., Gonzalez Canche, M. S., & Stollberg, R. (2016). Early RCT Findings for ELL Elementary Student Learning Outcomes After a Two-Year Pedagogical Intervention. SREE Spring 2016 Conference.
title: Instructional Conversation (IC) theory of change: conversational, cognitively demanding small-group pedagogy improves ELL achievement through interaction of cognitive and second-language development
description: The Instructional Conversation is described as "a complete classroom pedagogy that focuses on teaching through small-group dialogue with students allowing responsive instruction for each student." Its theory of change predicts that once the IC's critical components are well implemented, responsive assistance can significantly improve ELL academic achievement, working through the interaction of cognitive and second-language development produced by conversational experiences framed around specific academic goals. The model aims to promote higher-order thinking skills contributing to reading comprehension through mediated learning activities, and is anchored by cognitive-developmental and cultural-historical theory (Vygotsky).

Focused small group learning experiences providing ELLs ample opportunity for language output
Teacher time to model standard forms of language and give feedback helping learners notice correct forms

target_learning_goals: Standardized achievement in ELA, Math, Science, and other content areas
examples: Experimental teachers received a year of professional development, an initial intensive week of PD, two full-day fall renewals, and coaching feedback throughout the practice years, with logs and videotaped small-group lessons for both groups.

article_title: Interactive Projector as an Interactive Teaching Tool in the Classroom: Evaluating Teaching Efficiency and Interactivity
citation: Li-Ying Liu, Meng-Tzu Cheng. (2015). Interactive Projector as an Interactive Teaching Tool in the Classroom: Evaluating Teaching Efficiency and Interactivity. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(2). http://www.tojet.net/
title: A three-role coding system for classroom interactivity: ICTs as object, participant, and tool
description: The study developed a coding system defining classroom interactivity as "actions which are performed by teachers and students once they perceive the supported features of educational technologies". Building on Kennewell and Beauchamp's framework of 20 actions, it distributes actions into three categories by the role ICTs play: object (interact about ICTs, e.g. selecting, comparing), participant (interact with ICTs, e.g. annotating, questioning), and tool (interact through ICTs, e.g. composing, editing). Actions are scored 1-3 points by category, and efficiency ratings weighted by occurrence yield an effective score.
requirements: Actions must be observable in classroom video recordings and coders must reach consensus on category definitions and action descriptions
constraints: Developed and applied in middle-school biology lessons with an interactive projector; the authors note prior dialogue-focused methods miss the technology as a third interacting subject
target_learning_goals: Biology learning (digestive system) and classroom interactivity during technology-supported instruction
examples: Two researchers independently coded 22 clips for the general group and 28 for the interactive group, recording each observed action, its frequency, and a 0-4 teaching-efficiency rating

title: Three ICT-supported animated short narratives for the 6th-grade Force and Motion unit

description: This principle captures the article's own recommendation following its null and negative academic findings. The study found no academic growth from IC-JPAs in math while engagement and willingness to participate with peers increased, leading the authors to state that "This instructional strategy should be used with caution when teaching academic material and may be better suited for teaching conversational skills and social-emotional needs." citation: Hendy, Elizabeth and Cuevas, Joshua Dr. (2020). The Effects on Instructional Conversations on English Language Learners. Georgia Educational Researcher: Vol. 17 : Iss. 2 , Article 5. https://digitalcommons.georgiasouthern.edu/gerjournal/vol17/iss2/5
title: Instructional Conversation (IC) pedagogy combined with Joint Productive Activities (JPAs)
description: The Instructional Conversation pedagogy centers on educational discussion in which "the teacher adjusts their side of a conversation toward what they believe a student is trying to say about a topic," with teacher and student working together through conversation to form an authentic idea or conclusion. Combined with Joint Productive Activities (JPAs), students complete a content-related task through collaboration and conversation, creating a tangible product such as a t-chart. What distinguishes IC-JPAs from other classroom collaboration is the emphasis on students creating their own conversational goals, leading the conversations, and working together toward the product. The framework aims to build learning through educational conversations and relationships rather than pencil-and-paper work, and to bridge social-emotional learning and academic content in one cohesive activity.

Students must determine their individual conversational goals for the activity before beginning
constraints: The teacher is not an active participant in students' conversations; students take responsibility for asking one another questions and discussing the topic
examples: In the study, each IC-JPA lesson began with students sharing conversational goals, then students completed tasks such as creating a t-chart or a sort by conversing about the academic content while the teacher listened and assessed with minimal contribution

article_title: Research on Group Learning and Cognitive Science: A Study of Motivation, Knowledge, and Self-Regulation in a Large Lecture College Algebra Class
citation: David Miller and Matthew Schraeder. (2015). Research on Group Learning and Cognitive Science: A Study of Motivation, Knowledge, and Self-Regulation in a Large Lecture College Algebra Class. The Mathematics Educator, Vol. 24, No. 2, 27-55. https://tme.coe.uga.edu/
title: Interactive, Compensatory Model of Learning (ICML)
description: The ICML is a framework for understanding and improving classroom learning consisting of five components: cognitive ability, knowledge, metacognition, strategies, and motivation, with knowledge, metacognition, and strategies combined into a knowledge-regulation component. The article states it "captures the interactions between these four components (Cognitive Ability, Cognition, Regulation, and Motivation) that affect learning and describes how one component can compensate for deficiencies in others." Correlation coefficients from prior empirical studies are attached to the links, with knowledge-regulation to learning the strongest at 0.6. The authors use ICML to interpret why the middle prior-knowledge group benefited most from SP.
requirements: A measure of prior knowledge (the old ACT exam) to classify students into knowledge levels for applying the compensatory analysis
constraints: The correlation coefficients are estimated values from prior empirical studies cited by Schraw and Brooks (1999), not measured in this study
target_learners: college students in large lecture introductory mathematics courses
examples: The authors used ICML to explain that middle experimental students compensated for weaker prior knowledge with a stronger motivation component, strengthening knowledge through an iterative process across the semester
key_sources: David Miller and Matthew Schraeder. (2015). Research on Group Learning and Cognitive Science: A Study of Motivation, Knowledge, and Self-Regulation in a Large Lecture College Algebra Class. The Mathematics Educator, Vol. 24, No. 2, 27-55. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085089

article_title: Linguistic Outcomes of English Medium Instruction Programmes in Higher Education: A Study on Economics Undergraduates at a Catalan University
citation: Ament, J. R., & Pérez Vidal, C. (2015). Linguistic outcomes of English medium instruction programmes in higher education: A study on economics undergraduates at a Catalan university. Higher Learning Research Communications, 5(1), 47-68. http://dx.doi.org/10.18870/hlrc.v5i1.239
title: ICLHE versus EMI: an integrated content-and-language approach differs from content-only English medium instruction
description: The article distinguishes ICLHE (Integrated Content and Language in Higher Education) from EMI as two models of English-medium teaching at university. In ICLHE, "language outcomes are on the agenda as well as content," whereas EMI is content-focused with no language support and is explicitly English. The study's Catalan economics classes are classified as EMI rather than ICLHE because there reportedly is no focus on form and no translation or dialogue in Catalan or Spanish. The authors use this distinction to interpret why linguistic gains were limited.
requirements: For ICLHE as described, language outcomes must be explicit programme goals alongside content learning
constraints: The study's classes are EMI, not ICLHE: no focus on form, no translation or dialogue in Catalan or Spanish, and lecturers are not language specialists
target_learners: undergraduate economics students in a Catalan university studying through English
target_learning_goals: English as a third or additional language: grammar, listening, lexico-grammatical knowledge, and written complexity, accuracy, and fluency
examples: The Economics department's degrees range from 1500 EMI hours per year (IBE) to tracks offering 0 to 650 EMI hours, with all materials provided in English
key_sources: Ament, J. R., & Pérez Vidal, C. (2015). Linguistic outcomes of English medium instruction programmes in higher education: A study on economics undergraduates at a Catalan university. Higher Learning Research Communications, 5(1), 47-68. http://dx.doi.org/10.18870/hlrc.v5i1.239

article_title: Promoting Scientific Literacy by Using ICT in Science Teaching
citation: Al-Rsa'i, M. S. (2013). Promoting Scientific Literacy by Using ICT in Science Teaching. International Education Studies, 6(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n9p175
title: ICT tool set used in the experimental Astronomy and Space Physics course
description: The experimental group's instruction employed a specific set of ICT tools briefed to the course instructors: e-mails, Facebook and Twitter, on-line conference, and a learning site including YouTube-Cosmo Learning, space.com, universetoday.com, astronomynow.com, and astronomy101.jpl.nasa.gov. Instructors were also "trained on how to teach through employment of ICT using planning an educational tasks and worksheets by exploratory context". This tool set operationalised the ICT-based teaching whose literacy outcomes the study measured.
requirements: Colleagues teaching the course were trained and informed about the objectives and methodology of the study and familiarized with ICT tools
target_learning_goals: scientific literacy about space and astronomy concepts
examples: The learning site listed YouTube-Cosmo Learning, http://www.space.com/, http://www.universetoday.com/, http://www.astronomynow.com/, and http://astronomy101.jpl.nasa.gov/.

title: Iceberg Model of competency as the HLC-N's theoretical framework
description: The study adopted the Iceberg Model from competency theory (Spencer & Spencer) as its framework, distinguishing surface-level observable competencies from underlying attributes. "The Iceberg Model distinguishes between surface-level observable competencies (e.g., skills, behaviors) and underlying, less visible attributes (e.g., knowledge, attitudes, motivation)." The authors argue this hierarchical structure aligns with the multidimensional nature of nurses' health literacy competencies, and map the five-dimensional scale structure onto the model's levels (knowledge → skills → self-concept → traits → motivation).
requirements: Used as a framework for item generation and dimension structure rather than an empirically tested pathway model
constraints: The article states the hierarchical pathways of the Iceberg Model were not empirically tested
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of health literacy competency

article_title: Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education.
citation: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8
title: ICU Simulator browser-based multi-device simulation platform
description: ICU Simulator is a browser-based, client-side learning environment built with standard web technologies that "does not require local installation, a dedicated server, a database, or commercial software licenses." It integrates deterministic simulation modules for mechanical ventilators, patient monitors, infusion pumps and CRRT systems with a host interface and an AI-supported analysis panel, running at approximately 60 Hz. It was designed as a preparatory environment for biomedical device technology students.
requirements: Runs on standard computers via a web browser; designed for classroom demonstrations, computer-laboratory sessions and individual study
constraints: The platform is limited to predefined devices and quick findings; illustrative status indicators are simulation-generated and not validated performance metrics
examples: Pilot students completed at least one representative fault scenario from each of the four device modules in a supervised 40-minute session
key_sources: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8

citation: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8
title: Scenario-based fault analysis across four device modules with 18 fault patterns
description: The simulator includes "18 device-related fault patterns organized into scenario-based learning activities across four device modules": ventilator (airway obstruction, low compliance, circuit leakage, auto-PEEP), monitor (overdamping, underdamping, electrode disconnection, electromagnetic noise), infusion pump (line occlusion, free flow, air bubbles, low flow) and CRRT (filter clotting, blood line occlusion, effluent line problems, air detection, pump failure, sensor drift). Each scenario follows an observation–hypothesis–verification–interpretation pathway.
requirements: Scenarios require instructor supervision and guiding questions rather than direct answers
constraints: Scopes are limited to selected mechanisms and parameter relationships; scenarios are model-based educational representations, not full clinical variability
examples: In airway obstruction, peak pressure increases while plateau pressure remains relatively stable, indicating increased resistive load

article_title: From anatomy to surgical safety: scenario-based learning for internal carotid artery patterns in undergraduate education.
citation: Bedre Duygu Ozden, Govsa Figen, Yagdi Tahir, Duygu Ibrahim, Ozer Mehmet Asim, Gokmen Gokhan. (2026). From anatomy to surgical safety: scenario-based learning for internal carotid artery patterns in undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10076-2
title: Four-category geometric classification of cervical ICA patterns
description: The article classifies the anatomical geometric patterns of the cervical segment of the internal carotid artery into four categories: straight (no angulation), tortuosity (15–60 degrees), kinking (90–145 degrees), and coiling (360 degrees). The authors state these configurations "were chosen because they represent the most clinically recognized variations of the cervical internal carotid artery and encompass a broad spectrum of geometric, hemodynamic, radiological, and surgical characteristics". The classification structures both the training scenarios and the expert question-and-answer framework, providing what the article calls "a systematic structure from an educational perspective".
requirements: CT angiography imaging and angle-based morphological criteria to distinguish patterns, e.g., kinking forms a sharp angle between 90° and 145° versus smooth tortuosity curves
constraints: Classification applies to the cervical segment of the ICA as represented in the selected archive cases
target_learning_goals: classifying ICA variation patterns and understanding their hemodynamic and surgical implications
examples: Each of the four patterns anchored one clinical case scenario, from a 45-year-old woman with a straight ICA to a 65-year-old man with a 360° coiling at the C2 level.
key_sources: Bedre Duygu Ozden, Govsa Figen, Yagdi Tahir, Duygu Ibrahim, Ozer Mehmet Asim, Gokmen Gokhan. (2026). From anatomy to surgical safety: scenario-based learning for internal carotid artery patterns in undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10076-2

article_title: A comparison of student evaluations of teaching and learning in the inverted classroom model versus traditional lectures in dental education.
citation: Reuter Ann Katrin, Deschner James, Schütz Laura, Morlock Lisa. (2026). A comparison of student evaluations of teaching and learning in the inverted classroom model versus traditional lectures in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09733-3
title: Implement the inverted classroom model as a complement to traditional teaching, with institutional support and careful attention to cognitive load in early-stage learners
description: The article recommends that the ICM "can promote student engagement, interaction and flexibility", but that "careful implementation is required, particularly in the early stages of study, to avoid overload and ensure appropriate support for self-directed learning". Blended learning approaches integrating ICM elements "appear promising but should be implemented with institutional support, including technical infrastructure and pedagogical training for teaching staff". The ICM may complement rather than replace traditional teaching approaches.
requirements: Institutional support including technical infrastructure and pedagogical training for teaching staff
Careful implementation to avoid overload and ensure appropriate support for self-directed learning, particularly in the early stages of study
constraints: The findings relate to a single course in the early stages of dental education at a single institution, and transferability to other disciplines, educational levels or institutional settings remains uncertain
The results should be interpreted as associative due to the quasi-experimental design, with no randomised allocation
target_learners: first-year dental students in the preclinical phase
examples: First-year dental students experienced 15-minute asynchronous video preparation followed by 30-minute interactive face-to-face sessions weekly over 12 weeks, compared with 45-minute traditional lectures delivered by the same two lecturers.
key_sources: Reuter Ann Katrin, Deschner James, Schütz Laura, Morlock Lisa. (2026). A comparison of student evaluations of teaching and learning in the inverted classroom model versus traditional lectures in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09733-3

article_title: Cultivating competent public health professionals: the role of research participation and academic motivation.
citation: Wang Xinyu, Li Xinquan, Zhang Jiahui, Bao Sihan, Bian MaoWang, Sun Jiabin, Cai Weiqin, Xiao Yang, An Hongqing. (2026). Cultivating competent public health professionals: the role of research participation and academic motivation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09145-3
title: McClelland's Iceberg Model frames job competency as visible knowledge and skills above the surface and deeper intrinsic traits below
description: The article uses McClelland's competency theory (Iceberg Model) to interpret how research participation improves job competency. The model "divides human capabilities into two distinct parts: the visible knowledge and skills 'above the surface,' and the deeper, underlying intrinsic traits such as motivation, self-concept, attitudes, and values hidden 'below the surface'." Research participation is argued to cultivate both surface-level technical skills and deeper intrinsic qualities such as resilience, critical thinking, and intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Competency evaluation must capture both surface-level knowledge/skills and deeper intrinsic traits for the framework to be meaningful
constraints: The model is used as an interpretive lens rather than directly tested in the study
target_learning_goals: Development of both technical competencies and deeper intrinsic professional qualities
examples: The article links surface-level cultivation to literature review, experiments, data analysis, and report writing, and deeper cultivation to resilience, stress tolerance, and proactive responsibility

article_title: Development status of young new farmers from the perspective of vocational ability: A research analysis based on 21 cities in Guangdong Province.
citation: Luo Tao, Huang Qingpeng, Mai Jingyan. (2026). Development status of young new farmers from the perspective of vocational ability: A research analysis based on 21 cities in Guangdong Province. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349224
title: Three-level iceberg model of vocational ability for young new farmers.
description: The study proposes an iceberg model classifying professional competencies into three interrelated levels: surface layer professional skills (production and operation management), middle layer general skills (communication, organizational management, practical innovation), and deep layer core competencies (social responsibility, learning ability, sustainable career development). This framework was operationalized through a 50-item questionnaire and used to compare farmers across disciplinary backgrounds. The model draws on career construction theory, career adaptability theory, occupational identity formation theory, and the capability approach.
requirements: Requires multi-dimensional assessment instruments covering all three levels
constraints: Developed and validated specifically for the young new farmer population in Guangdong Province
examples: Applied through a 50-item 5-point Likert scale questionnaire with dimensions for professional skills, general skills, core competence, and career sustainable development ability

citation: Gull Ambreen, Yasmin Rahila, Mahboob Usman, Golnik Karl C., Moin Muhammad. (2026). Validation of the ICO-OCEX tool for competency-based assessment in ophthalmology residency programs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09154-2
title: ICO-OCEX: a 34-item workplace-based assessment tool with four constructs and a three-point Dreyfus rubric
description: The ICO-OCEX (International Council of Ophthalmology-Ophthalmic Clinical Evaluation Exercise) is a workplace-based formative assessment tool consisting of 34 items measuring four constructs (Interview Skills, Examination Skills, Interpersonal Skills, Case Presentation Skills) on a three-point Dreyfus scale ('novice, beginner, competent'). It employs 'behaviorally descriptive milestones based on the Dreyfus model to address inconsistent grading interpretations.' The finalized instrument with behavioral descriptors and rating rubric is provided as supplementary material.
requirements: Faculty orientation and training for consistent application
constraints: Intended for clinical, non-procedural patient encounters only; does not evaluate surgical competence
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of interview, examination, communication, and case presentation skills

article_title: Simulation-based learning enhances interprofessional competencies in undergraduate health students: a retrospective pre-post study.
citation: Gomwe Howard, Phiri Lesego, Marange Chioneso Show, Kgongwana Thokozile Harriet, Zikalala-Mabope Lindi, Mothapo Rahab, Dyani Xolelwa. (2026). Simulation-based learning enhances interprofessional competencies in undergraduate health students: a retrospective pre-post study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09125-7
title: Interprofessional Collaborative Competency Attainment Survey (ICCAS) as a retrospective pre-post measure
description: The ICCAS, developed by MacDonald et al., is a 21-item survey measuring perceptions of interprofessional learning, with 20 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale covering six competencies: communication, collaboration, roles and responsibilities, patient-centred approach, conflict management, and team functioning. Each item is rated both before and after the learning activity, "enabling a comparison of students' perceived competencies over time". The article reports strong internal consistency (total Cronbach's alpha 0.919 pre-test, 0.890 post-test) and cites prior validation work reporting alpha coefficients from 0.92 to 0.96.
requirements: Administered retrospectively after the intervention, with each item rated for both before and after the learning activity
constraints: Relies on self-reported perceptions, so self-reporting bias cannot be excluded
examples: Used with N = 540 first-year students across nursing, medicine, pharmacy, allied health, dental and emergency medical care programs in Gauteng, South Africa

article_title: Perceptions and Enhancement Needs of Psychiatric Nurses on Patient Safety Competency: A Phenomenological Study.
citation: Shen Chen, Xu Lihua, Jiang Qianyun, Li Yumei. (2026). Perceptions and Enhancement Needs of Psychiatric Nurses on Patient Safety Competency: A Phenomenological Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/3736316
title: Iceberg Model of competency as a framework for exploring psychiatric nurses' patient safety perceptions
description: The study adopts McClelland's Iceberg Model of competency as its theoretical framework, in which "Knowledge and skills represent the visible portion of the 'iceberg,'" while motivation, personal traits, attitudes, values, and self-concept lie beneath the surface. The authors used the model to structure research questions (surface-level knowledge and skills versus deep-level values and motivations) and to design the interview guide, moving "from 'visible' to 'invisible' and from 'concrete' to 'abstract'" to build trust and reduce defensiveness. It frames patient safety competency as more than observable behavior, encompassing deep-level drivers of safety practice in mental health settings.
requirements: Interviewing that progresses from concrete facts and behaviors to subjective feelings, values, and core needs
constraints: Applied in this study specifically to psychiatric nurses' perceptions of patient safety competency in closed inpatient wards
target_learners: Registered psychiatric nurses with at least one year of psychiatric clinical experience
target_learning_goals: Patient safety competency: knowledge, attitudes, and skills to prevent adverse events and avoid patient harm
examples: The interview outline was designed and the interview process controlled according to the model's surface-to-deep principle

citation: Rao Lijia, Wu Jiahua, Deng Bixia, Hong Yubing, Wu Juan, Chen Yiming, Chen Mu. (2026). Efficacy of a hybrid case-based learning and simulated clinical encounter model versus lecture-based learning in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08937-x
title: ICAP framework account of the hybrid model's engagement shift
description: The article frames its hybrid model with the Interactive–Constructive–Active–Passive (ICAP) framework, which "posits that shifting students from Passive listening to Active, Constructive, and Interactive modes leads to deeper learning outcomes". LBL places students in a passive role, while the hybrid model's role-play and case discussion place students in Interactive and Constructive modes, which the authors offer as the mechanism behind the clinical thinking and communication gains.
requirements: Learning activities must move students beyond passive listening into interactive and constructive engagement modes
constraints: The framework is applied here as an interpretive account; the study did not measure engagement modes directly
target_learners: undergraduate dental students in preclinical training
examples: Students role-played Dentist and Patient, collected history, performed simulated tests, and explained diagnosis and treatment plans

citation: Zhang, Limei; Zhong, Xiaoying; Liu, Jing; Yuan, Tingting; Yang, Wenli; Wang, Meng; Yuan, Ping; Ding, Xing. (2026). Analysis of Correlation Between the Core Competency Status and Spiritual Health of Nursing Intern Students. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/3522503
title: Iceberg model of competence as the framework explaining how spiritual health underpins core competencies
description: The article applies the iceberg model of competence, in which ability has a two-layer structure: explicit attributes (knowledge and skills), the "visible part of the iceberg," and implicit personal attributes such as motivation, traits, and self-image, the "underwater part of the iceberg," which is the core of ability. The authors use it to explain how spiritual health, as an implicit factor, shapes both layers: it drives intrinsic motivation, professional identity, and core values, and fosters interpersonal connections that yield learning resources and skills. The model frames the study's hypothesis that spiritual health predicts core competencies.
requirements: Used for interpreting relationships between implicit personal traits (spiritual state) and observable professional abilities in nursing education research
constraints: The article presents it as an explanatory lens for the observed correlations, not as a causally tested mechanism
target_learners: nursing intern students in clinical practice
target_learning_goals: professional competence development, professional identity, intrinsic motivation
examples: The authors interpret the r = 0.687 correlation and the 42.9% variance explained through the model's implicit-attribute layer

article_title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Scale for Disaster Rescue Nurses in Mainland China.
citation: Lai Jinjia, Chen Hongyi, Huang Yongqi, Ma Chaoqun, Zeng Ping, Chen Hanxi, Tan Yibing. (2025). Psychometric Evaluation of the Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Scale for Disaster Rescue Nurses in Mainland China. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/9957270
title: ICN Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Version 2.0: an eight-domain, three-level competency framework for disaster nursing
description: The CCDN V2.0, published by the International Council of Nurses in 2019, is a competency framework for disaster nursing that the article describes as "a comprehensive framework outlining eight essential domains for disaster nursing: preparation and planning, communication, incident management, safety and security, assessment, intervention, recovery, and law and ethics". It stratifies competencies into three levels based on nurses' roles and responsibilities, with Level II nurses defined as any nurse who has achieved Level I competencies and is or aspires to be a designated disaster responder. The framework articulates 33 core competencies at Level II and serves as the basis from which the CCDNS-DRN was translated and validated. The article positions it as an aspirational benchmark guiding improvement of disaster nursing education worldwide.
requirements: Adaptation into a validated, population-specific assessment scale (as done here for Chinese DRNs) to enable direct measurement, since the framework itself had lacked psychometric evaluation in China
constraints: The article states the standard it sets "is often higher than the current practical level of disaster nursing education" and functions as an aspirational goal
target_learners: Disaster rescue nurses at Level II; more broadly nurses at three role-based levels
target_learning_goals: Disaster nursing core competencies across the framework's eight domains
examples: The study transformed the Level II nurse competency requirements in CCDN V2.0 (8 domains, 33 items) into the Chinese-language CCDNS-DRN and retained the eight domains as latent variables in CFA

article_title: Student motivation and instructional clarity: Linking experience sampling method data to objective behavioural observations.
citation: Oschwald, A., Moeller, J., Kracke, B., Viljaranta, J., & Dietrich, J. (2025). Student motivation and instructional clarity: Linking experience sampling method data to objective behavioural observations. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S281–S299. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12775
title: Qualitative coding manual for instructional clarity with three indicators
description: A high-inference rating system was developed, blending deductive and inductive approaches, to code lecturers' instructional clarity from video recordings at three-minute intervals synchronized with ESM signals. "The rating system comprised three items: two positive indicators measuring the amount of detail (depth) and variation (width) in the explanation, and one negative indicator measuring the logical consistency of the argumentation." Two independent raters coded 238 observation intervals; an overall composite rating was abandoned due to low variance of the negative indicator.
requirements: Moderate inter-rater reliability achieved through manual refinement on video material excluded from analyses; two independent raters.
constraints: The authors note the high-inference multi-item approximation to low-inference coding may lose important aspects of validity, and that averaging three intervals before a beep reduces variance.
target_learning_goals: objective observation of instructional clarity as a situational teaching-quality characteristic
examples: Inter-rater reliability reached sufficient data quality: detail ICC = .62–.75, variation ICC = .55–.70, logical inconsistency ICC = .53–.69 (95% confidence intervals).

citation: Zhou Ailin, Li Zhourong, Wang Tiankun, Wu Rongxin, Yang Shuang, Shi Zumin, Zeng Huan, Zhao Yong. (2024). Development of the Competency Evaluation Scale for Clinical Nutritionists in China: A Delphi Study. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162593
title: Iceberg model of competency as the theoretical basis for scale development
description: The iceberg model of competency, first proposed by McClelland, divides competencies into visible surface characteristics such as knowledge and skills and latent characteristics such as traits, social roles, and motivation. The article uses it as the theoretical basis for the scale: "using the iceberg model as the theoretical basis for scale development will allow for the consideration of the complexity and diversity of competency components". Accordingly, the scale's five dimensions are grouped into penetrance characteristics (professional theoretical knowledge, professional practical skills) and intrinsic characteristics (humanistic practice, interpersonal communication, professional development).
requirements: Competency components must be mappable to both visible (knowledge and skills) and latent (traits, social roles, motivation) layers of the model
constraints: The article applies the model in the context of clinical nutritionist competency assessment in China
target_learning_goals: professional competency assessment covering knowledge, skills, humanistic practice, communication, and professional development
examples: The scale's five primary indicators were mapped onto the model: the first two as explicit competencies and the latter three as implicit ones
