article_title: Enhancing academic performance and student engagement in health education: insights from Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA).
citation: Sánchez Judit, Lesmes Marta, Rubio Margarita, Gal Beatriz, Tutor Antonio S. (2024). Enhancing academic performance and student engagement in health education: insights from Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05478-z
title: ICAP framework: four engagement modes (interactive, constructive, active, passive) predicting learning outcomes
description: The ICAP framework, introduced by Chi and Wylie, "categorizes learning tasks based on the nature of student engagement," identifying four modes: interactive (discussion and collaboration with others), constructive (generating new ideas or applying learned concepts), active (direct manipulation of materials), and passive (observation without participation). It proposes that as engagement deepens, learning outcomes improve. This study used ICAP as the basis for a systematic classroom observation instrument to classify WSLA students' engagement and relate it to grades.
requirements: Observable student behaviors during activities that can be reliably categorized into one of the four engagement modes
constraints: The study required a predominant behavior (75% internal criterion) and excluded students with mixed or conflicting behaviors, leaving only 156 of 466 possible cases classifiable
target_learning_goals: characterizing the nature of student engagement during active learning activities
examples: Researchers observed student groups at 2-minute intervals during WSLA sessions, marking engagement categories and classifying each student by predominant behavior

article_title: Real-Time multifaceted artificial intelligence vs In-Person instruction in teaching surgical technical skills: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yilmaz Recai, Bakhaidar Mohamad, Alsayegh Ahmad, Abou Hamdan Nour, Fazlollahi Ali M., Tee Trisha, Langleben Ian, Winkler-Schwartz Alexander, Laroche Denis, Santaguida Carlo, Del Maestro Rolando F. (2024). Real-Time multifaceted artificial intelligence vs In-Person instruction in teaching surgical technical skills: a randomized controlled trial. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-65716-8
title: ICEMS: a multifaceted deep-learning system providing real-time surgical instruction and risk detection
description: The Intelligent Continuous Expertise Monitoring System is described as "a multifaceted multi-algorithm deep learning system with a rapid-decision capability for real-time applications" designed to mimic human expert surgical instructors during simulation training. It comprises six long-short term memory network algorithms — one for objective skill assessment and five for risk detection and feedback — and "assesses surgical performance in 0.2-s intervals and provides real-time instruction and risk detection" on five metrics: bleeding risk, tissue injury risk, aspirator force, bipolar force, and using the two instruments together. In this trial it delivered real-time auditory instructions when a learner's score deviated more than one standard deviation from expert level for at least one second, plus post hoc 10-s error video clips.
requirements: Requires integration with a simulator providing continuous performance data; in this study it was integrated into the NeuroVR (CAE Healthcare) virtual reality platform with two haptic handles.
constraints: The current version was designed for learners with limited knowledge of brain tumor surgery; continuous task assessment may not accurately reflect procedural outcome, and assessments focus more on instrument handling than operative outcomes.
target_learners: Medical students with little to no surgical exposure (years one to four of medical school)
target_learning_goals: Bimanual psychomotor surgical skills, specifically simulated subpial brain tumor resection technique
examples: In the trial, ICEMS delivered six real-time auditory instructions during practice tasks and generated up to six 10-s post hoc error video-clips per repetition, with five minutes of post hoc feedback for all groups.

article_title: Effect of active learning and online discussions on the academic performances of dental students.
citation: Lim Jaeseo, Ko Hyunwoong, Park Jooyong, Ihm Jungjoon. (2022). Effect of active learning and online discussions on the academic performances of dental students. BMC Medical Education, 22, 312. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03377-9
title: ICAP framework: active engagement modes before discussion produce richer learning than passive modes
description: The article applies Chi and Wylie's Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive (ICAP) framework, which "describes four cognitive active learning engagement modes", with the passive mode referring to "calmly sitting in traditional lectures" and the other three modes involving segmented active learning methods. The study uses ICAP to predict that self-study (a more active mode) before discussion beats lecture (a passive mode), and reports that its findings support the framework in an online dental education setting.
requirements: Learning activities must be classifiable into engagement modes so that more active pre-discussion activities can be selected
constraints: The article tests ICAP's prediction in one online experiment with dental students on a non-health topic; the authors note future studies are needed to expand and generalize the findings
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes from active engagement modes preceding discussion
examples: The study predicted the self-study mode would be more effective than lecturing because it is more active and productive, following ICAP

article_title: Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning.
citation: Hilton, C. B., Goldwater, M. B., Hancock, D., Clemson, M., Huang, A., & Denyer, G. (2022). Scalable Science Education via Online Cooperative Questioning. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-11-0249
title: ICAP-framed account of question answering as active and question authoring as constructive engagement
description: The article uses the ICAP framework to explain why authoring questions should benefit learning more than answering them. "the ICAP framework (Chi and Wylie, 2014), whose acronym describes a hierarchy of modes of cognitive engagement in terms of their benefit to learning—interactive > constructive > active > passive." Authoring a high-quality MCQ requires harmonizing many relations among stem, options, examples, and audience, drawing on generation, self-explanation, and analogical comparison; cooperative feedback adds an interactive mode. The framework describes the means of learning, complementary to Bloom's taxonomy, which describes the ends.
requirements: Supporting activities that scaffold deeper engagement, since unscaffolded authoring risks superficial knowledge-telling
constraints: The article reports that teachers struggle with implementing interactive learning experiences in particular
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding and knowledge restructuring
examples: The study operationalized engagement depth as a 0–3 authoring score keyed to Bloom levels, plus peer-feedback comments in the cooperative step.

article_title: Does group size matter during collaborative skills learning? A randomised study.
citation: Noerholk LM, Morcke AM, Kulasegaram K, Nørgaard LN, Harmsen L, Andreasen LA, Pedersen NG, Johnsson V, Vamadevan A, Tolsgaard MG. (2022). Does group size matter during collaborative skills learning? A randomised study. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14791
title: ICAP framework applied to collaborative clinical skills training
description: The ICAP framework classifies learners' overt behaviours into four modes of cognitive engagement: passive, active, constructive and interactive, each associated with different examples of learning activities. The article states that "The ICAP framework describes a hierarchical distribution of learning activities, where interactive activities are thought to be superior to constructive activities, which are superior to active activities, that again are superior to passive activities (I > C > A > P)." The study translated these modes into a numeric coding scheme (0–4) and rated recorded training sessions minute by minute to compare learning activities across group sizes.
requirements: Video recording of training sessions and a locally adjusted ICAP coding scheme to rate activities minute by minute
constraints: The authors note the framework categorises observation as passive regardless of cognitive engagement level, which may undervalue the role of observation for learning practical skills
target_learning_goals: complex procedural and diagnostic skills such as obstetric ultrasound
examples: The study coded 120 one-minute time periods per participant and scored the highest ICAP activity displayed in each period; inter-rater ICC (3,k) was 0.70.

article_title: Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course.
citation: Leupen, S. M., Kephart, K. L., & Hodges, L. C. (2020). Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-06-0112
title: ICAP framework as an account of engagement levels in group learning
description: The article adopts Chi's ICAP framework (interactive, constructive, active, passive) as its theoretical lens for why some team talk promotes learning. Passive behaviors only transmit information; active engagement connects information to prior knowledge; higher-order learning arises from constructive and interactive behaviors: "constructive" or "interactive" behaviors "involve students in making inferences, either individually or collaboratively, respectively". The article maps its observed discourse phenomena onto this framework, treating re-evaluation and co-construction as markers of interactive engagement.
requirements: Group tasks that prompt students to generate inferences rather than passively receive information
constraints: The framework is used interpretively in this study; it was not itself tested empirically here
target_learning_goals: Higher-order learning through constructive and interactive engagement
examples: Questions that prompt re-evaluation are described as pushing students into the ICAP interactive mode

article_title: Authoritative parenting stimulates academic achievement, also partly via self-efficacy and intention towards getting good grades.
citation: Hayek J, Schneider F, Lahoud N, Tueni M, de Vries H. (2022). Authoritative parenting stimulates academic achievement, also partly via self-efficacy and intention towards getting good grades. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265595
title: Dual-process / I-Change account of the direct and cognition-mediated influence of the home environment on adolescent achievement
description: The article uses the I-Change Model as its framework for socio-cognitive determinants of achievement, combining it with a dual-process view of environmental influence. It states that "environmental factors, in this case parents, can have a direct automatic influence on behavior and an indirect mediated effect via behavior-specific cognition". In this account attitude, social norms and self-efficacy shape intention, which is treated as the primary determinant of behavior; the study's serial mediation model operationalises this pathway from parenting style through self-efficacy to intention to achievement.
requirements: Measurement of the socio-cognitive constructs (attitude, social norms, self-efficacy, intention) alongside the environmental factor and the outcome, as done with the I-Change-based questionnaire
constraints: Applied here to parenting style and academic achievement in Lebanese adolescents; the article notes attitude and social norms did not significantly predict achievement in this context
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement (school grades) and the motivational cognitions supporting it
examples: The serial mediation model tested parenting style (X) → self-efficacy (M1) → intention (M2) → academic achievement (Y) with Hayes PROCESS model 6

article_title: Data-rich textbook figures promote core competencies: Comparison of two textbooks.
citation: Finby B, Heyer LJ, Malcolm Campbell A. (2021). Data‐rich textbook figures promote core competencies: Comparison of two textbooks. Biochem Mol Biol Educ. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21488
title: Integrating Concepts in Biology (ICB) textbook
description: Integrating Concepts in Biology is a commercial introductory biology textbook written de novo by the authors around Vision and Change and AP Biology redesign recommendations. Each chapter is organized around one core concept and one size scale, and "a pedagogical device in ICB called “integrating questions” asks students to analyze and interpret published data," so students practice scientific process and quantitative analysis while learning core concepts. Its figures and tables were found to be data-rich, question-associated, and interpretive.
requirements: Requires students to answer Integrating Questions using information in figures and tables themselves
constraints: Commercial book sold by Trunity, not free to all students, which the authors state limits access; publisher offers reduced pricing and scholarships
Limited to English only, limiting accessibility for international students
examples: Evaluated in its summer 2016 edition against the 6th edition of Biological Sciences by Freeman et al.

title: ICM periodontology module pattern: self-study preparation followed by small-group case discussion of digitized patient cases with lecturers as mediators
description: A lesson-level design combining the inverted classroom with case-based learning: students first acquire declarative knowledge via lectures, slides and self-study on an e-learning platform, then attend two four-hour units in which each student classifies a real digitized patient case (staging and grading), develops a patient-specific treatment concept, and presents and discusses it in small groups. examples: 55 students classified 33 digitized patient cases whose correct classifications were determined beforehand by three experienced periodontists, then re-classified after small-group discussion

title: Use ICM-based case teaching as a supplement to, not a replacement for, patient-based learning in clinical dental education
description: The article's central design recommendation: inverted-classroom case-based teaching can build diagnostic confidence and support procedural skills acquisition for complex topics, but it cannot replace the clinical experience gained by treating real patients. The authors state "The ICM-based teaching concept is definitely not an alternative to patient-based learning" yet conclude the module "may be a useful addition to traditional dental education in future curricula". The principle therefore positions ICM case teaching alongside clinical treatment courses.

constraints: Correct classification of periodontal patients requires clinical experience and procedural knowledge acquisition that the ICM format cannot adequately compensate for
target_learners: dental students in clinical phase of training
examples: The module was introduced as a substitute during patient-free pandemic teaching, and the authors still recommend it as an addition to, not a substitute for, patient-based education
